The marker dropped its licence because MIT's condition is the full copyright and permission text, which `.bkit/LICENSE.md` carries; a URL in each file (what PolyForm's Notices section accepted) satisfies nothing under MIT.

summary: Superseded by `mit-licence-everywhere`: one licence (MIT) for every payload folder, and the marker names no licence
A red for an unchanged test stands on resume; a red refused as `passed` blocks the task; already-landed and moved tests are not gaps when the evidence says so
description: `bkit tests red` returns `already: true` without running when a red exists for the same task, test file and test name and the file hash is unchanged. Refusals carry a kind (`no-report`, `not-run`, `passed`, `skipped`, `exit-mismatch`); execute blocks on `passed` and never undoes code to force a red. Execute skips reds for tasks logged `DONE — already landed`; verify reads the plan-currency report and maps that `no-red` to no gap. `tests green` reports whether a recorded test the plan does not name passes now, so verify can clear a renamed or moved test.
rationale: Execute never ticks tasks, so a resumed build re-runs it from the first task and every finished task would otherwise be refused and loop. Work that already landed cannot show a red. A test moved by plan-currency `Reword` leaves the planned path missing, which gap-remediate cannot fix. Found by a full read of every workflow and prompt that touches plan tasks.

summary: bkit ships no context-compression proxy (caveman, Headroom) and no proxy template; token cost is cut by reading less (`.agents/rules.md` `Code reads` / `Narrow text search first`, ReadGuard)
description: Measured in `tests/compression/bkit-caveman-headroom-compression-proxy-comparison.md`: 456 Claude Code transcripts from one consumer repo, 500 tool results replayed offline with their real tool call and user message. Projected share of total cost saved, bootstrap 95% range: caveman 1.8% (1.0–2.6%), Headroom with Kompress off 0.8% (0.4–1.4%), Headroom with Kompress 2.7% (2.2–3.2%). Both proxies keep the prompt cache intact: each tool result is compressed once on arrival and the same compressed form is resent on later requests. Tool results >= 2 KB, re-reads included, are 26.9% of cost; the rest (agent messages, system prompt, rules, tool definitions) is not rewritten while the cache is warm. Exact repeats of an earlier result are 2.1% of cost, bounding lossless de-duplication. Not measured: Headroom's default `--mode token` and its opt-in `HEADROOM_DEDUPE` / `HEADROOM_COLD_RECOMPACT`.
rationale: About 1–3% saving does not justify an extra process in every session that sees all LLM traffic. The larger savings are lossy: Kompress changed code syntax (`(preset) => void` became `(preset) void`), caveman elides function bodies, and one live caveman run produced a wrong answer from a compressed log. Reading less is lossless and reaches the share a proxy cannot.
alternatives: Ship Headroom `--mode cache --disable-kompress` as an optional template (rejected: 0.8% saving, one more moving part); caveman (rejected: every bkit agent's `tools:` needs its retrieve tool, voice harms written artifacts); Headroom with Kompress (rejected: rewrites code).

summary: Audit reports record their audited commit in the same `bkit:anchor` block as design and plan docs; filenames keep the UTC timestamp suffix, not a commit hash
description: `@bkit-audit-generate` stamps `<!-- bkit:anchor -->` (`baseSha` = HEAD at stub creation, `baseRef` = audited branch via `bkit branches anchor-stamp --base-ref=`) on top of the report right after creating it, so the commit is machine-readable at the top of the file instead of in Step 1 prose. Each template Step 1 reads the previous report commit from its anchor, falling back to the HEAD its `Previous Run` recorded. A hash in the filename was rejected: the same commit is audited more than once (re-runs, audits of live outside state such as open dependency PRs, model catalogues, CI timings) so it is not unique, and hashes do not sort by time, which Step 1 relies on to find the newest prior report. Plan and design filenames stay fixed (`{FID}-plan.md`, `{FID}-design.md`): workflows open them by exact name, `-plan-*` means split sub-plans, and they already carry `baseSha` in their anchor.

summary: `maxTurns` gets a fourth tier, XL=300, held only by `@bkit-audit-generate`
description: One agent runs all 35 audit templates and the cap is set per agent, so the audit runner moves from L=150 to a new XL=300 tier rather than splitting into per-template agents. Measured local runs: log-triage 177 turns (cut off with no final reply, work also split across four helper agents of 47-98 turns), security 175, prompts 141, friction 139, harvest 60. Big audits do real work past 150, so L was acting as a workload budget for them; XL sits at about twice the largest measured run, the same doubling the 3600s step timeout uses.
alternatives: 200 (rejected: the largest measured runs already reach ~177); a second XL audit agent for the big templates only (rejected: a second agent rendered per host, a launcher that must pick per template, and a big-template list that goes stale, for no gain beyond stopping a stuck small audit sooner)

summary: Audits probe every tool they need before the probe steps and pause on a blocked call; the audit agent hands back narrow allow rules instead of finishing with silent gaps
description: `@bkit-audit-generate` has no tool for asking a human, and in Claude Code auto mode its frontmatter `permissionMode` is ignored, so each action goes to the classifier and a blocked call surfaces only as a `Not Checked` row at the end of the run. Each template Pre-Flight now opens with a `Permissions` item: one cheap read-only call per tool the run uses, blocked calls recorded verbatim with the narrow allow rule that clears them, never retried or reworded to get past the block. The audit prompt stops before `Probe Steps` when any call was blocked and hands back those rules; the caller grants them and resumes the agent, or resumes it with `continue`. Blocked calls persist in the template `Project Instructions` `Permissions` list so the next run probes them first. Allow rules over chat approvals: a chat approval clears one named action, and whether a subagent classifier reads approvals given to the parent session is undocumented.
alternatives: An up-front ask by the launching session in `.agents/rules.md` (rejected: audit-runner behaviour belongs in the audit prompt and templates, not the universal rules); continuing with gaps and no pause (rejected: the run spends its whole budget and still lacks the evidence a one-minute grant would have given)

summary: bkit-audit-generate appends MEDIUM+ findings to docs/failures.jsonl and closes rows a rerun no longer finds; plan and design pick them up through the existing ledger scan
description: Audit findings lived only in the report, so /bkit-plan saw them only when the issue named the report (AUDIT_PATHS), and they dropped out of sight once the next run replaced the report. The audit agent now writes each MEDIUM+ finding as a failure row keyed audit-{slug}-{content-slug}; a rerun reuses the key for the same problem, re-severities via append, and closes open audit-{slug}-* rows it no longer finds when it checked their surface. The failures and deferrals audits write nothing. AUDIT_PATHS stays for plans that fix one report.
rationale: failures.jsonl is the known-bugs backlog plan Step 4 and design already scan, and bkit-utility-update-failures already closes fixed rows, so no new search step or staleness logic is needed. deferrals.jsonl is wrong: a deferral is chosen-to-postpone work with a required reason, and audit findings would skew the unjustified-deferral rate. LOW findings are mostly wording and would crowd the scan. Report finding IDs are renumbered per run, so keys are content slugs.
alternatives: Plan Step 4 scans docs/audits/ and matches finding Location against the draft plan files - rejected: new search step, own staleness filter (baseSha), and findings still vanish when a report is replaced.

summary: Script-host guardrails (Cursor, Codex, Antigravity) classify git by the parsed command; Claude and opencode carry glob rows for the common git reorderings in the same tier; --no-verify is ask-tier everywhere; shell reads of secret files are gated on the script hosts only
description: `hooks/guardrails-tiers.js` parses each segment, `sh -c` script and `$(…)` substitution: git global options skipped, flags in any order, short clusters expanded, option values never read as flags. DENY: `git push` with `--force`, an `f` in a short cluster, or a `+refspec`; `--force-with-lease` never. ASK: `git reset --hard`, any `git clean` that is not `-n` / `--dry-run`, whole-tree `git checkout` / `git restore` (not `--staged` alone), `git stash drop`, `git rebase -i` / `--interactive`, `git filter-branch`, `--no-verify` on any git subcommand, `git commit -n`; plus a `secret` tier for a shell read of `.env` / `.env.*` (not `.env.example`), `*.pem`, `*.p12`, `id_rsa` — redirect targets, copy destinations, grep / rg patterns, comments and `ls` / `mv` / `test`-style commands are not reads. Cursor and Antigravity ask on it, Codex advises. Claude `permissions` and opencode `permission.bash` add glob rows for the same tiers (`git push * --force`, `git push * -f*`, `git push * +*`, `git reset *--hard*`, `git clean -*f*`, `git checkout *.`, `git restore *.`, `git * --no-verify`, …); they carry no rows for shell secret reads. The Claude guardrails hook stays advisory-only.
rationale: Prefix rows and literal regexes let `git reset -q --hard`, `git clean -df`, `git push origin +dev` and `git push origin dev --force` through on every host. Claude globs take `*` anywhere, so reordered force-push is expressible as deny without touching `--force-with-lease`; the Claude hook therefore needs no deny / ask decision, which keeps `guardrails-shell-advisory-scope-and-detection`. Only force-push is deny: the permissions deny list is global to every agent Bash call, and `.agents/rules.md` permits `--force-with-lease` on personal branches. opencode is last-match-wins, so its new ask rows for `--no-verify` sit after the `git push --force-with-lease*` allow and its anywhere-force deny rows after those, keeping the existing keys so no consumer migration is needed. Claude and opencode get no shell secret-read rows because a command-text glob such as `Bash(* .env *)` also matches `cp .env.example .env`, `git add .env.example`, grep patterns and commit messages, and an ask stalls autonomous and cloud runs on those harmless commands, which costs more than the read it would catch.
alternatives: Make the Claude PreToolUse hook return deny / ask — rejected: globs express the force-push cases, and a hook decision is a second policy source. Shell secret-read glob rows on Claude and opencode (`Bash(* .env *)`, `Bash(*.pem *)`, `Bash(* id_rsa *)`) — rejected: they cannot tell a read from a mention and stall unattended runs. Mass-promote the PROHIBITED git list to deny — rejected by the tier split above.

summary: bkit-audit-generate appends MEDIUM+ findings to docs/failures.jsonl, reusing any open row that names the same problem whichever workflow wrote it, and closes only its own audit-{slug}-* rows a rerun no longer finds
description: Audit findings lived only in the report, so /bkit-plan saw them only when the issue named the report (AUDIT_PATHS), and they dropped out of sight once the next run replaced the report. The audit agent now writes each MEDIUM+ finding as a failure row. Matching runs against every open row, not only audit-{slug}-* keys: debug runs, triage and other workflows already record most flakes and many bugs under their own keys, and a prefix-only match wrote a second row for the same problem on every run (worst on the flakes audit, whose subject is rows the ledger already holds). Same problem = same file:line, test title or error signature; a match reuses that key, otherwise a new audit-{slug}-{content-slug} key is minted. Closing stays scoped to audit-{slug}-* rows so a rerun that misses an intermittent flake never closes a row another workflow opened. The failures and deferrals audits write nothing. Templates that named failure rows as a later step now say the audit agent writes them. AUDIT_PATHS stays for plans that fix one report.
alternatives: Plan Step 4 scans docs/audits/ and matches finding Location against the draft plan files - rejected: new search step, own staleness filter (baseSha), and findings still vanish when a report is replaced. Exempting the flakes audit from ledger writes like failures and deferrals - rejected: flakes no other workflow recorded would never reach the ledger, and security and testing hit the same duplication.

summary: Audits probe every tool they need before the probe steps but never stop on a blocked call; they run everything the remaining tools allow and list blocked calls, their narrow allow rules and the skipped work under Not Checked
description: `@bkit-audit-generate` has no tool for asking a human, and in Claude Code auto mode its frontmatter `permissionMode` is ignored, so each action goes to the classifier. Each template Pre-Flight opens with a `Permissions` item: one cheap read-only call per tool the run uses. A blocked call, there or in any later step, is recorded verbatim with the narrow allow rule that clears it in `Not Checked`, `Process Improvements` and `Project Instructions` `Permissions`, never retried or reworded; the run carries on with every step the remaining tools allow and lists the work it could not do under `Not Checked`. Blocked calls persist in `Project Instructions` `Permissions` so the next run probes them first and the owner has one list of rules to grant. The earlier stop-and-resume pause is dropped: some blocks are deliberate (an owner who will not grant a production read), and a pause assumes every block is cleared by an allow rule, so those runs stopped before Step 1 on every run and an unattended run waited forever. Allow rules over chat approvals: a chat approval clears one named action, and whether a subagent classifier reads approvals given to the parent session is undocumented.
alternatives: Stop before Probe Steps and hand back allow rules to grant, or resume with continue (rejected: stalls every run on a deliberately blocked call and every unattended run); a known-gap marker in Project Instructions that exempts a call from the pause (rejected: keeps the pause and adds a per-project switch to fix a problem not stopping removes); an up-front ask by the launching session in `.agents/rules.md` (rejected: audit-runner behaviour belongs in the audit prompt and templates, not the universal rules).

summary: The outdated-bkit warning lives in `bkit repo info` and the anchor stamp, not in a rules.md rule or a prose step per workflow / audit template
description: Every phase workflow's Step 1 already runs `bkit repo info`, and every design, plan and audit doc is already stamped by `stampAnchor` (`bkit workflows promote` / `bkit branches anchor-stamp`). Both compare `.bkit/version` `pinnedVersion` (the release the workflow, prompt and template text was rendered from) with the newest published `@cbartens/bkit`, compared as numbers with a prerelease older than its release. `repo info` returns `bkitAdvisory`, which Step 1 shows the user; the stamp records `bkitVersion` / `bkitLatest` in the anchor block and, when outdated, writes a visible tool-owned `Outdated bkit` line under it, so a doc read later shows it came from stale templates. Warning only: no registry answer, no pin, or `BKIT_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` means no warning, never a failure. The registry is asked at most once a day (cache in the git common dir, failures remembered for an hour) so parallel runs and offline runs add no wait. The pinned version is compared rather than the installed package because the rendered text, not the binary, is what an agent reads.
alternatives: A rule in `.agents/rules.md`: an instruction the agent may skip, the semver comparison is error-prone by hand, and it loads in every session including ones that run no workflow. A prose step in each phase workflow and each `docs/templates/bkit-audit-*.md`: the same steps copied into every file and every consumer, drifting apart. An opt-in `--bkit-version` flag on `anchor-stamp` for audits only: leaves design and plan docs without the record.

summary: `maxTurns` tiers become S=50 / M=100 / L=200 / XL=400; the five ledger and roadmap utilities move to XL
description: Human-set brackets. L rises 150 to 200 for the test-loop source modifiers; XL rises 300 to 400 for `@bkit-audit-generate`. `@bkit-utility-update-decisions`, `-deferrals`, `-failures`, `-knowledge` and `-roadmap` move from M=100 to XL=400: each re-checks every row of a whole ledger (or the whole roadmap board) against code, docs and tracker, so their turn count grows with ledger length rather than with one task. Replaces `audit-generate-xl-turn-tier` on the cap value only; the cap stays a runaway-loop guard, not a workload budget.
alternatives: keep ledger utilities at M=100 (rejected by human: whole-ledger sweeps outgrow 100 as ledgers grow)

summary: `maxTurns` tiers become S=50 / M=100 / L=200 / XL=400; every `bkit-utility-update-*` agent and both maintainer release agents sit at 400
description: Human-set brackets. L rises 150 to 200 for the test-loop source modifiers; XL rises 300 to 400 for `@bkit-audit-generate`. All six `@bkit-utility-update-*` agents (decisions, deferrals, failures, knowledge, roadmap, documentation) move from M=100 to XL=400: each re-checks a whole ledger, the roadmap board or the doc catalog, so their turn count grows with what they sweep rather than with one task. The maintainer-local release agents `utility-new-release` (was 100) and `utility-pre-release-check` (was 200) also move to 400. Replaces `audit-generate-xl-turn-tier` on the cap value only; the cap stays a runaway-loop guard, not a workload budget.
alternatives: keep the update utilities at M=100 (rejected by human: whole-surface sweeps outgrow 100 as ledgers and docs grow)

summary: `maxTurns` tiers are S=50 / M=100 / L=200 / XL=400; S holds only `*-summary`, L adds every codebase-sweeping investigator and whole-doc rewriter, XL holds the audit runner, every `bkit-utility-update-*` agent and both maintainer release agents
description: Human-set brackets; the cap is a runaway-loop guard, so agents with any recorded early stop or codebase-wide work move up one bracket. 100 to 200: `@bkit-build-plan-verify` (stopped at 50 tool uses, findings unwritten), `@bkit-ship-deferred-sweep` (70 + 75 tool uses across a resume), `@bkit-debug-failure-diagnose` (56 and 74 tool uses, only the template saved), `@bkit-plan-generate` (budget spent on research, skeleton only), `@bkit-plan-update` and `@bkit-design-update` (whole-doc rewrites ending at Verdict: PENDING), `@bkit-build-challenge-1/-2` (cut off in final bookkeeping), `@bkit-build-challenge-reconcile`, `@bkit-build-challenge-tests`, `@bkit-build-plan-current` (same diff surface), `@bkit-design-spike` (runs probe code), `@bkit-ship-update-docs` (per-cycle twin of update-documentation). 50 to 100: `@bkit-plan-scope-check-1/-2`, `@bkit-plan-complexity-check` (read the whole plan against code), `@bkit-debug-abort-handover`, `@bkit-build-install-skills`. L also rises 150 to 200 for the test-loop modifiers; XL rises 300 to 400 for `@bkit-audit-generate`; all six `@bkit-utility-update-*` agents move 100 to 400 because each sweeps a whole ledger, the roadmap board or the doc catalog; `utility-new-release` (100) and `utility-pre-release-check` (200) move to 400. Early-stop counts come from `.bkit/friction.jsonl` and `harvest/friction.jsonl` and count tool uses, not turns, mostly from runs under the older 25/50 caps. Replaces `audit-generate-xl-turn-tier` on the cap value only.
alternatives: raise only agents with a recorded cap hit (rejected by human: the cap is only a ceiling, so codebase-wide work moves up without waiting for a hit); keep the reviewers and ideators at 100 too (kept: they read a few docs and write one, no recorded hit); L=150 so the `@bkit-build-plan-execute` cap stays a sharp signal that a plan should have been split (#463 body; superseded by the human choice of 200 — the cap still bounds an oversized plan and `@bkit-plan-complexity-split` remains the upstream control)

summary: `.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json` and `.opencode/opencode.json`: bkit owns only its tracker entry, and inside it only the keys and toolsets the template sets; extra keys, headers and toolsets are the consumer's
description: Install and upgrade reset each key the template sets in the tracker entry and keep the consumer's other keys and headers (`mergeTrackerEntry`, `.bkit/core/engine/install/write.ts`). `headers["X-MCP-Toolsets"]` keeps the consumer's list in its order and appends any template toolset it lacks, so a toolset bkit adds still reaches every consumer. The entry is in sync, and `bkit check` reports no drift, when it already holds everything that merge would write (`trackerEntryInSync`). Used by `reconcileMcpJson` (`.mcp.json`, `.cursor/mcp.json`) and `reconcileOpencodeJson` (`mcp.<tracker>`). The rest of each file stays the consumer's, as before. Uninstall is unchanged: it removes the entry only while it still equals the template, so an extended entry stays.
rationale: bkit owns the entry because tracker steps run through it, and those steps need only what the template sets: the URL, the `Authorization` header and the `issues` / `projects` toolsets. The whole-entry exact match also refused additions that cannot break any step, so enabling one more toolset (consumer-a adding `actions` in Cursor and OpenCode) needed a bkit release, and `bkit check` failed pre-push and CI until then (#613).
alternatives: Exact match on the whole entry (the previous rule) — replaced: it refused harmless additions. Template wins on the toolset list — rejected: the list is one comma-separated string, so a plain merge drops every consumer toolset. Consumer list replaces the template list — rejected: a toolset bkit adds would never reach existing installs, and an old install missing `projects` would stay broken.

summary: Vulnerability, config and secret scanning ships as one copy-and-own Trivy workflow, `bkit-trivy.yml`, running the official image pinned by tag and digest
description: `bkit-trivy.yml` runs `trivy fs --scanners vuln,misconfig,secret --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --exit-code 1 --include-dev-deps --skip-dirs .bkit/templates` on push, pull request and a daily cron, through `uses: docker://ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy:<tag>@sha256:<digest>`. Acceptances live in `.trivyignore.yaml` (`statement` + `expired_at`), passed only when the file exists. With `scripts/ci/check-dependency-audit.mjs` adopted the scan skips `pnpm-lock.yaml`, so a pnpm advisory is accepted in `accepted-advisories.json` only. No `bkit check` advisory and no setup tip for an absent scanner.
rationale: Renovate and Dependabot propose fixes and never fail CI; the pnpm audit gate covers pnpm lockfiles only. Trivy is the one open-source tool covering lockfiles in every language, container and IaC config, and secrets in a single pinned binary. The docker image pinned by digest lets Renovate bump tag and digest together, where a binary download needs a sha256 no updater refreshes. `aquasecurity/trivy-action` and `setup-trivy` tags were re-pointed at a credential stealer in March 2026, so no tag-referenced action. `--include-dev-deps` is required: measured on this repo, Trivy 0.75.0 without it read 0 of 193 pnpm packages and passed.
alternatives: OSV-Scanner: lockfiles only; image scanning less mature; a second tool once containers arrive
Grype + Syft: comparable image scanning; ignore rules carry no expiry
Extend check-dependency-audit.mjs to read Trivy JSON: one acceptance file for every stack, but more code; deferred until a non-pnpm consumer needs a dated-acceptance gate
trivy-action / setup-trivy pinned by SHA: still runs the action install path hijacked in March 2026

summary: The capstone's pass/fail verdict is `scripts/ci/check-capstone.mjs`, required with `bkit-ci.yml`; the template capstone step reds with a copy-the-script message when the file is missing, and never skips itself
description: `check-capstone.mjs` reads the lanes from `LANES` plus `<LANE>_RESULT` / `<LANE>_RAN` / `<LANE>_CACHE_SKIP`, an optional `PLAN` and `SCOPE_RESULT`, and `EMPTY_COUNT`. It reds on a lane whose result is not `success`, a lane that ran under `run_level=none`, a lane that succeeded with 0 tests or a non-numeric count, a plan that does not parse, a failed scope job and an empty `LANES`. `cache_skip=true` and `run_level=none` with every lane skipped assert nothing. No `PLAN` means every listed lane is expected to run. The template sets `EMPTY_COUNT: warn` so a lane that writes no count yet stays a warning; bkit's own workflow leaves it unset, so an unreported count reds. Both workflows run it after an ungated checkout without `continue-on-error`. `ci-scripts.test.ts` runs the script's test file and asserts both capstone steps call it with every `needs` lane wired in; bkit's `scripts/ci/` copy stays byte-identical to the template (`dogfood-templates.test.ts`). The whole-file snapshot of the template workflow is replaced by targeted assertions.
rationale: The assert is the only required check and a shell block inside YAML cannot be unit-tested: changing the 0-test arm survived the full suite in bkit's workflow and was caught in the template only by the whole-file snapshot. A missing script must red because skipping the step would leave a green that proves nothing. The template and bkit's copy are copy-and-own files that `bkit install` and `bkit upgrade` never write, so no migration exists to add the script to a consumer; a consumer sees the changed template path on upgrade and copies it.
alternatives: Skip the step when the script is absent: rejected, green proves nothing
Keep the inline shell and test it by extracting it from YAML: rejected, the test would copy the code it guards
Migration that writes the script into a consumer's scripts/ci/: rejected, the workflow and scripts are copy-and-own and no install path writes them
Gate the checkout on the plan: rejected, a run with no script exits on a missing module before reading the plan

summary: Shell guardrails flag off-allowlist curl/wget URL hosts and shell-as-edit-channel writes as advisories; Claude's hook never denies or asks; detection is head-of-command-line, scheme-strict, host-only, quote-aware, covers nested commands on every host and is quiet on scratch sinks
description: `.claude/hooks/bkit-guardrails.cjs` covers only what a command-prefix permission table cannot express: URL hosts and shell edits into source files. It emits `additionalContext` only. Cursor's twin asks on off-allowlist fetches and allows shell edits with an agent_message; Codex's emits its ask tier as advisory. All hosts share one shell parser (`hooks/guardrails-shell.js`: `shellWords`, `commandWords`, `commandLines`) and match the program of every command line it yields — each list / pipeline segment, `sh -c` script and `$(…)` / backtick body — not a bare token, so a fetch or in-place edit inside a wrapper is caught. They count only explicit-scheme URLs, consult only each URL's host, and report only unquoted redirects into repo-looking paths with source extensions.
rationale: Claude rules match a command prefix, never a URL host, and a blanket ask row would force a prompt on every shell fetch in every mode — unanswerable in a cloud session; the hook gives the signal without the prompt. `deny` already lives in settings.json and is evaluated before any hook, so a duplicate would be dead code with a second place to drift. A content-scoped `ask` is evaluated before the auto-mode classifier and always forces a prompt — the stall the host is configured to avoid. Shell edits stay advisory on every host because the edit-tools rule has sanctioned exceptions (bkit's plan workflow does a `sed -i.bak -E` bulk rewrite) and a gate that blocks a documented exception gets switched off. Matching a bare token fires on `grep 'curl'`, and a gate that fires on noise or constantly is one consumers disable. A scheme-less token cannot be told apart from a local path without guessing, and guessing turns a flag into an allow. Matching the allowlist against the whole command string is defeated by `?src=github.com` or `github.com.attacker.io`; the host alone decides where bytes go. On Codex the ask tier informs rather than stops; every command in it is already PROHIBITED in all bkit workflow headers, so only a human driving Codex by hand reaches it. Two shell parsers (a segment-head splitter for fetch / edit, a quote-aware one for git tiers) let `sh -c 'curl …'`, `$(curl …)` and `(curl …)` slip past the fetch gate and read a `>` inside quotes as a file write; one parser in the part every host includes closes both.
alternatives: Ask row on Claude shell curl — rejected: prompt on every fetch. Block shell edits — rejected: sanctioned exceptions. Whole-string allowlist match — rejected: trivially defeated. Keep the segment-head splitter beside the quote-aware parser — rejected: wrapped fetches bypass the gate and a quoted > reads as a write.

summary: The local static gate (bkit:gate:static) and the CI bkit-tests-static job run the same steps, including pnpm lint; a test fails when they diverge
description: bkit:gate:static chains typecheck, lint, format:check, lint:prose and slop:delta. The template bkit-ci.yml static job runs a Run Lint step (pnpm lint) after Run Typecheck, so a push that skips the hooks (cloud agent, --no-verify, web edit) is still linted. template-ci-yml.test.ts splits the gate into its pnpm scripts and asserts each has a run: pnpm <script> step in bkit-tests-static (slop:delta may carry an argument); exceptions live in a named list with a reason each. An adopted bkit-ci.yml is copy-and-own, so existing consumers keep their copy; no migration ships.
rationale: The template already told non-Node users to replace its typecheck / lint / test steps, and the local gate runs pnpm lint unconditionally, so any repo that passes the local gate has a lint script and the CI step cannot break it. Keeping lint local-only leaves every push that bypasses hooks unlinted.
alternatives: Keep lint local-only and document the gap: unlinted pushes land from cloud agents, --no-verify and the web UI.

summary: The gate-config file-name list lives only in .bkit/core/hooks/gateguard-engine.js, the code every host hook inlines; the TypeScript copy, its generator and the generated .cjs are gone
description: gateguard-engine.js holds GATE_CONFIG_PATTERNS and isGateConfig and is inlined into each host hook, so it is the list that decides whether an edit gets the weaken-the-gate advisory. shared/protected-paths.ts keeps only MIRROR_PATH_PREFIXES and isMirrorPath for the compliance grader. Gate-config cases are asserted in audits/hooks/gateguard-parity.integration.test.ts against the generated hook of every host, so a pattern dropped from the engine fails a test. The removed .claude/hooks/gate-paths.generated.cjs existed only in bkit's own repo, install never wrote it and .claude/ is not in the npm package, so no consumer migration is needed.
rationale: The TypeScript list had 13 patterns against the engine's 23 and no production caller; its drift test compared a generated file nothing executes, so it stayed green while the live list changed. One list tested through the real hooks cannot diverge from itself.
alternatives: Generate the engine's pattern list from the TypeScript table at render time: adds a build step and a second place to edit for a list the hooks already own.
Keep both lists and widen the drift test to compare them: the TypeScript copy would still have no caller.

summary: bkit-cloud.yml is disabled in bkit's own repo (repo setting) rather than wired to runner secrets; the workflow file is unchanged
description: The dogfood copy of the cloud lane no-ops unless ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_PROVIDER_KEY is set, and neither is. It is disabled with gh workflow disable bkit-cloud.yml (gh workflow list --all shows disabled_manually) and re-enabled with gh workflow enable bkit-cloud.yml once a key is set as a repo secret. docs/deployments.md records this under the bkit-cloud.yml section.
rationale: Putting an LLM provider key into repo settings is a credential decision for the owner. Disabling needs no credential and is undone with one command.
alternatives: Set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_PROVIDER_KEY as repo secrets so the lane runs live: needs the owner to choose and store a credential.
Delete .github/workflows/bkit-cloud.yml: loses the dogfood copy of the shipped template.

summary: The unit coverage gate lives in one package.json script that both bkit's CI unit lane and /bkit-build Run Tests run; its branch floor lives in vitest.unit.config.ts
description: `test:coverage:unit` in `package.json` carries `--coverage.include` and `-c vitest.unit.config.ts`, which holds `coverage.thresholds.branches`; `Run Unit Tests` in `.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` and the /bkit-build Run Tests step (via `bkit:gate:static-unit`) both call it; the CI step only appends the JSON reporter + outputFile for the executed-count. `Report Unit Coverage` reads the same file via `vite-config-path` and runs on every event, so the job summary shows the measured figure against the floor on pushes as well as PRs.
rationale: vitest stays the gate (one run, no custom gate script), and the floor has one file read by both the gate and the report: a CLI flag in package.json cannot be scraped by the report action, and a floor written twice drifts. A coverage drop still fails in the build worktree before CI sees it.

summary: The shipped bkit-stub:coverage unit report runs on every event and reads the unit floor from vitest.unit.config.ts
description: `.bkit/templates/.github/workflows/bkit-ci.yml` bkit-stub:coverage: `Report Unit Coverage` has `if: !cancelled()` plus a `hashFiles` guard on the unit summary, `vite-config-path: vitest.unit.config.ts`, and `comment-on: pr` on same-repo PRs else `none`. The stub and `.bkit/shared/docs/testing.md` § Coverage on PRs put the unit floor in a `vitest.unit.config.ts` loaded with `-c` by the unit run only; the `--coverage.thresholds.branches` CLI flag is no longer the recommended form. The `coverage` advisory in `.bkit/core/engine/checks/after/tools.ts` says the same.
rationale: davelosert/vitest-coverage-report-action always writes its table to the job summary and shows a floor only when it can scrape `<metric>: <number>` from a file; a CLI flag cannot be scraped, and the PR-only guard left pushes with no statement of the floor at all. vitest stays the gate, reading the same file, so the shown floor is the one that gates. Copy-and-own template: no migration.

summary: One readInstallingVersion() in shared/package-json.ts throws when bkit's own package.json is missing, not a JSON object, or has no string version
description: `readInstallingVersion(root = getPkgRoot())` in `.bkit/core/engine/shared/package-json.ts` is the only reader of the version of the bkit package doing the install, built on `readPackageJson`. It throws an Error naming the file and saying to reinstall `@cbartens/bkit` when `package.json` is missing, is not a JSON object, or has no non-empty string `version`. Every former copy (`install/placeholders.ts`, `checks/after/managed.ts`, `install/modules/core.ts` x2, `commands/install/install.ts` x2, `checks/before/index.ts`, `commands/install/upgrade.ts`) calls it; the install.ts `getInstallingVersion` and core.ts `readInstallingVersion` wrappers are gone. `commands/comply.ts` `readBkitVersion` keeps its own fail-open walk-up: the compliance grader never gates.
rationale: The file is bkit's own manifest inside the installed package, so a damaged one means a corrupt install, not a consumer mistake. The old `"0.0.0"` fallback fed a wrong value into the stamp, the pin and the gates: markers rendered as v0.0.0 while the `.bkit/version` pin write threw, and `detectManagedStale` returns null on `0.0.0`, which switches the stale-marker gate off exactly when the install is broken. Six readers fell back and two threw, so one run could stamp half the files and then abort. Throwing stops before any file is written, matches the existing `package corrupt?` exit in `runCoreModule`, and surfaces through the CLI's top-level handler as one clear message. The `0.0.0` / empty guard in `detectManagedStale` stays for an injected unreleased-tree version.

summary: Unit tests may drive real git, bash and node against an os.tmpdir() folder; no network, no backing service
description: The Unit row of the docs/testing.md Tiers table allows real git / bash / node subprocesses run against a throwaway os.tmpdir() folder. It keeps the bans on network, backing services and state outside that folder. Driving the bkit CLI via tsx and wired multi-module flows stay Integration. About 33 non-mocking *.test.ts files under .bkit/core/engine/ spawn such processes; the commands/** ones are labelled Unit (boundary: real temp git repo).
rationale: The commands/** sources are thin wrappers over git, so a test that fakes git proves little. test:coverage:unit excludes *.integration.test.ts and holds the 78% branch floor in vitest.unit.config.ts, so renaming these files would drop their coverage from the floor and break it. Their slowness and timeouts belong to the flakes audit, not the tier line.
alternatives: Rename the files to *.integration.test.ts: drops them out of test:coverage:unit and breaks the branch floor.
Split the pure logic out of each wrapper into separate unit tests: large rewrite that duplicates what the real-git tests already prove.

summary: Test files are linted by Oxlint with oxlint-tsgolint, not ESLint, running only five test-quality rules as errors
description: `pnpm lint` runs `oxlint -c .oxlintrc.json --type-aware --tsconfig tsconfig.test.json --deny-warnings .bkit/core/engine`. `.oxlintrc.json` turns the default categories off and enables, for `**/*.test.ts` only: `vitest/expect-expect`, `vitest/no-conditional-in-test`, `vitest/no-conditional-expect`, `vitest/valid-expect` with `maxArgs: 2`, `typescript/no-floating-promises`, all `error`. Both packages are exact devDependencies (oxlint 1.87.0, oxlint-tsgolint 7.0.2004). `pnpm lint` sits inside `bkit:gate:static` and the CI static lane. No baseline, no ignore list: every hit is fixed in the test.
rationale: typescript-eslint 8.71.2 supports only TypeScript below 6.1.0 and the repo is on TypeScript 7.0.2, so type-aware ESLint rules such as `no-floating-promises` cannot run. oxlint-tsgolint is built on TypeScript 7 and runs the same rule. `valid-expect` defaults to one argument; Vitest's `expect(value, message)` is legitimate, so `maxArgs: 2` removes 122 false hits. Only these rules run because the issue is tests that cannot fail, and the default categories flag many unrelated things. oxlint 1.88.0 was younger than the 7-day `minimumReleaseAge` when chosen.
alternatives: ESLint with @vitest/eslint-plugin and typescript-eslint: no type-aware rules on TypeScript 7.
ESLint without type-aware rules: drops no-floating-promises.
Baseline or ignore list for existing hits: tests that cannot fail stay in the suite.

summary: bkit's own pnpm install refuses releases younger than 7 days and runs with supply-chain protections on, set in `pnpm-workspace.yaml`; the shipped Renovate example stays unchanged
description: `pnpm-workspace.yaml` sets `minimumReleaseAge: 10080`, `trustPolicy: no-downgrade`, `blockExoticSubdeps: true`, `strictDepBuilds: true` and `onlyBuiltDependencies: [esbuild]`. Every install, including lockfile-maintenance and automerge-group PRs, skips versions published in the last 7 days, direct and indirect. `devDependencies` are exact versions. The shipped Renovate example does not set `minimumReleaseAge`; it remains the consumer's choice per `docs/deployments.md`.
rationale: pnpm 11 can run out of memory on Mend's hosted runner, so the shipped example leaves the setting to the consumer. bkit runs Renovate on its own `ubuntu-latest` runner, which has the memory, so the repo can take the 7-day gate. `onlyBuiltDependencies` rather than `ignoredBuiltDependencies`: with `strictDepBuilds` on, pnpm 10.34.6 still fails the install with `ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS` for an ignored package, and `allowBuilds` is not read by that version; esbuild's postinstall only verifies and swaps in the platform binary, so letting it run is harmless.
alternatives: ignoredBuiltDependencies: [esbuild]: install fails under strictDepBuilds on pnpm 10.34.6
Renovate-only minimumReleaseAge: leaves local and CI installs ungated
Set minimumReleaseAge in the shipped Renovate example: risks pnpm 11 out-of-memory on Mend hosted runners

summary: `engines.node` is `>=24`, matching `.nvmrc`, CI and `release.yml`; it ships in the next major release
description: Node 20 and 22 are no longer supported. Consumers on them break on install, so the release carrying this change is a major version. `docs/technology.md`, `docs/setup.md`, `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `.bkit/README.md` state `>=24`; `CHANGELOG.md` lists it under Breaking Changes. `docs/migrations.md` does not list it because it registers code migrations only.
rationale: bkit is built, tested and released on Node 24 only, so a lower floor claims support nothing exercises.
alternatives: Keep >=20 and add Node 20 and 22 to the CI matrix: more CI cost for runtimes nothing needs
Raise the floor in a minor release: breaks consumers without a major-version signal

summary: The shipped Renovate example extends config:best-practices, rebases PRs only on conflict, holds majors for dashboard approval, runs lockfile maintenance monthly and tracks off-manifest pins through one regex custom manager
description: Both `renovate.json5` copies: `extends: ["config:best-practices", ":dependencyDashboard"]`; an npm packageRule restores `minimumReleaseAge: "7 days"` over the preset 3 days; `rebaseWhen: "conflicted"`; majors carry `dependencyDashboardApproval: true`; `lockFileMaintenance` runs before 6am on the first day of the month; `ignorePaths` repeats the `:ignoreModulesAndTests` entries and adds `docs/plans/**`; `packageManager` joins the non-major group; one `customManagers` regex reads `# renovate: datasource=... depName=...` comments in Dockerfiles, `.claude/bkit-cloud.md` and workflows. `bkit-renovate.yml` pins `renovate-version` and the github-actions lookup of `ghcr.io/renovatebot/renovate` is disabled.
rationale: The default rebase re-runs CI on every open automerge PR whenever the base branch moves. Majors otherwise open a branch and a CI run before anyone decides on them. ghcr.io image tags carry no publish date, so `minimumReleaseAge` would hold every renovate-version update as pending; GitHub releases are dated. A repo-level `ignorePaths` replaces the preset list rather than extending it. Checksum-paired pins get the version bump only; the sha256 is updated by hand in the same PR.
alternatives: Keep config:recommended: no digest pinning of Docker images and actions, no abandoned-package flags
Leave renovate-version floating: the action tag can sit a major behind the latest Renovate
rebaseWhen behind-base-branch: one CI run per open PR on every base push

summary: Push to dev blocked when docs/capabilities.md is not what the pushed commit builds; checked in a throwaway checkout of that commit; graphify absent only warns
description: graphify pre-push block: push to dev → bkit-graphify.sh check-at PUSH_DEV_SHA → exit 1 on drift. check-at builds in a git worktree of the pushed commit: graphify reads the working tree, so uncommitted edits (usually a concurrent session's) would otherwise decide the answer. graphify not installed → NOT-checked warning, push goes on: a cloud session that cannot install it must still push; CI Check Capability Register re-checks every push to dev. Revert pushes skip it, as they skip the test tiers. Other branches keep the warn-only staleness note. One graphify release (GRAPHIFY_SPEC in bkit-graphify.sh): register commands refuse others, CI installs it; another release draws different edges. Upstreamed from app-gether-life, whose owner decided the same on its #1467.
alternatives: Warn-only note (previous state: stale register reached dev, CI red on 08ecf9b6). Plain graph:check in the hook (reads uncommitted edits → another session can flip it red or green). Block when graphify absent (locks out cloud sessions without it).

summary: Network allowlist is core-owned .bkit/allowlist.json, written for every host set; a recorded .cursor/allowlist.json is migrated away, not kept as a fallback read
description: Cursor, Codex, Claude and Antigravity guardrail hooks read one allowlist. It lived at .cursor/allowlist.json and only the Cursor module wrote it, so a Codex-only or Antigravity-only install (or uninstall --cursor) flagged every fetch while bkit check stayed green. Core now writes .bkit/allowlist.json on every install and upgrade; it is a CORE_MANIFEST byte-equal entry, so bkit check drift-gates it and full uninstall removes it. Hooks find it from the payload workspace roots / cwd, walking up to the .git root, because Antigravity runs plugin hooks from the plugin directory. Upgrade deletes a .cursor/allowlist.json whose hash .bkit/version records and prunes the hash; an unrecorded file is left alone. Owner confirmed the layout change on 2026-10-19.
alternatives: Keep .cursor/allowlist.json and write it whenever any reader host is installed (host-named path owned by a different host; uninstall --cursor still has to know about readers). Read the old path as a fallback (stale copy never updated or removed).

summary: bkit:debug is a mutually exclusive phase label; every phase start drops next:* and bkit:failed; issues no workflow has started carry one next:<phase> or next:<phase>:lite; lite workflows are named <phase>:lite and set the same phase labels
description: The workflow label on an issue names its next best step (design -> plan, plan -> build, build/debug -> ship, failed -> debug), so an issue needs a next:* hint only before any workflow starts. bkit:debug was additive and never removed, so shipped issues kept a stale bkit:debug and its Linear state flipped to In Review at debug start. bkit:failed survived a re-run of the failed workflow. The label arithmetic in bkit issues labels keeps every label it does not recognise, so dropping next:* has to live there; a rules.md line alone would be undone by every workflow write. Lite workflows set the same phase labels so a next:<phase>:lite hint is cleared by the run it points to. Lite names flip to <phase>:lite so they match the next:<phase>:lite labels.
alternatives: Keep bkit:debug additive (the build/ship label shows what is being debugged, but nothing marks debug finished and the label goes stale). Drop next:* by rule only (workflow label writes put it back). Clear bkit:failed only at debug start and merge (a re-run carries a stale failure marker). Lite runs set no labels (next:<phase>:lite never clears).

summary: Every design / plan close builds its commit in a throwaway .worktrees/_land-{FID} off origin/dev and pushes HEAD:dev, retrying up to 10 times with 2s-doubling, 30s-capped, jittered backoff when dev moved; any other refusal falls back to the PR squash-merge, whose merge also retries after update-branch. The close takes no dev lock, local dev is only fast-forwarded (laptop, pure fast-forward, skipped otherwise), and Gate 12 reads status.jsonl from origin/dev.
description: Parallel design / plan sessions collided at close: each checked out, pulled and squashed into dev in the one shared main checkout, so another session's staged or uncommitted file, or a dev moved by a sibling close, failed the squash or the push. Building the commit off origin/dev in a private worktree removes the shared checkout from the critical section, so the only remaining race is the push itself, which a rebuild-and-retry absorbs. Cloud runtimes get the same routine: a runner that can push dev retries the race instead of failing, and a runtime whose push is refused (protected dev, claude.ai git proxy) falls back to the PR close with a retried merge. Because local dev may stay behind (local commits, an uncommitted edit the move would overwrite), the gate and the audit read the landed copy on origin/dev rather than the main checkout's file.
alternatives: Keep the local squash under the dev lock (serialises closes but still fails on another session's uncommitted or staged files in the main checkout); 3 push retries with no backoff (too few for several sessions closing together); make Gate 12 read the main checkout file and require the fast-forward (a skipped fast-forward would fail a close that landed).

summary: A production rollback moves production back to the last good deployment first (every production host, from a rollback workflow sharing the deploy job's concurrency group), marks the bad deployment in ROLLED_BACK_DEPLOYMENT_ID, then fixes forward with a revert through dev and a normal release. Force-resetting main is a last resort for commits a dev release cannot undo, run only after production is back. bkit-tests-deploy refuses a marked deployment and a commit that does not descend from the one production serves.
description: The runbook reset main first and moved the host last. The reset is a push to main, so with bkit-tests-deploy it started a release run before production moved; with an ancestry-checking deploy job (both consumers that adopted bkit-tests-deploy run one) every release refused until production moved, and without one the CI promote raced the manual host promote. Moving the already-built good deployment is the fastest mitigation and needs no git change; fixing forward keeps main equal to what was released and keeps branch protection on.
alternatives: Keep reset-first and add a warning (the ordering hazard stays the default path); reset main and let the reset's release run promote the good commit (rebuilds instead of reusing a proven build, and runs with branch protection off); ship a rollback.yml template (larger change; the runbook states what such a workflow must do, consumers own the host-specific switch).

summary: #341 OQ-A confirmed, OQ-D withdrawn: design/plan close lands through `bkit branches land` as a direct dev push of a squash built off origin/dev in every runtime, else (push refused) via a {BRANCH}->dev PR merged with gh (D5(a), not push_files); the landed subject keeps `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no CI
description: Design and plan Close Workflow run one `bkit branches land --workflow=<design|plan>` (`landVerb` in `.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/branches.ts`). Every runtime first tries the direct close (`landDirect` / `buildClose`): `git merge --squash -X ours {BRANCH}` in a throwaway `.worktrees/_land-{FID}` off a fresh origin/dev, roadmap row, one path-scoped `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` commit (`--squash-of={BRANCH}`), `git push origin HEAD:dev`, rebuilt and retried when dev moved (decision `design-plan-close-throwaway-origin-dev-worktree`). Any other push refusal (branch protection or a ruleset on dev) takes `landPr`: commit the roadmap update on {BRANCH}, push it, open or reuse the {BRANCH}->dev PR (`existing: "reuse"`), and squash-merge it with subject `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` and an empty body via gh, retrying a refused merge after `update-branch`; exit 80 at stage `open` / `merge` hands either step to MCP `create_pull_request` / `merge_pull_request`, then re-runs with `--pr` / `--merged-sha`; the landed SHA is the PR merge commit. Both paths then scan the landed commit BODY (subject excluded) and cross-check the transport; the `close-transport` row (`closeTransportRow`) is written when the main checkout holds the landed status file. The merge does not wait for CI: the landed subject carries `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no run. The OQ-D CI-cost reversal accepted at build (drop `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject) is withdrawn.
rationale: Spike B (closed, folded into the design) found push_files (D5) cannot express `merge --squash -X ours`, inlines full file content per call (non-repairable payload bloat), and inverts conflict semantics (branch-wins vs dev-wins) -- three defects that demote it from primary. D5(a) is uniform with ship's server-side merge and avoids the push_files payload/conflict/credential-coupling defects. OQ-D was reversed: a deliberate `bkit [skip ci]` on a docs-only SUBJECT is the CI-minutes convention, and stripping it also breaks ship's promotion-lag guard in `bkit branches switch`, which stops a ship (exit 82) when a local dev commit ahead of origin/dev lacks the token. The real defect is a token inherited into a squash BODY; every close passes an explicit --body "" and `bkit prs scan-body` scans the landed BODY only. `.bkit/core/engine/audits/workflows/skip-ci-subject-audit.test.ts` asserts both halves.
alternatives: D5 (push_files) as shape-A primary -- REJECTED per Spike B (non-repairable payload bloat, conflict-semantics inversion, credential coupling shared with gh's own flaky mode-3 auth). Dropping `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject (the original OQ-D) -- REJECTED on reversal: one full dev CI run per docs-only close and a broken ship promotion-lag guard; the inherited-token risk is met by an explicit empty squash body plus a landed-body scan.

The close takes no dev lock, local dev is only fast-forwarded (laptop, pure fast-forward, skipped otherwise), and Gate 12 reads status.jsonl from origin/dev.

summary: Ship's close (docs({FID}): ship DONE) and Failure Path record (chore({FID}): ship FAILED) are built by pushToDev in a throwaway .worktrees/_land-{FID} off origin/dev, carrying the run's book (md logs the checkout lacks copied, ledgers unioned), and pushed as dev with rebuild-and-retry when dev moved. Ship books in {WORKTREE_PATH} in every runtime; its workflow lock stays in the main checkout. The repo-global dev lock, bkit branches switch and every --dev-pushes flag are removed.
description: A laptop ship switched the main checkout to dev and committed there under a dev lock, so it could sweep another session's uncommitted work into its commit and serialised every parallel close. The design / plan close already proved the throwaway-checkout routine; ship now uses the same one, which removes the shared checkout from every dev write and leaves the push as the only race. The book moves to the feature worktree because the main checkout is no longer a tree ship may write to; the lock stays in the main checkout because it is gitignored and must be one file whichever tree the run books in.

summary: bkit workflows close --flush --branch= removes the workflow-created feature worktree and deletes the branch only after the close is on dev (kept while a close PR is unmerged); ship's Step 14 Worktree Cleanup and its ship-worktree-cleanup step key are retired, Close Workflow becomes Step 14 and ends with cd {REPO_ROOT}, and Gate 14 reads status.jsonl from origin/dev.
description: With the book in the worktree, removing the worktree before the close would delete the rows the close commit must carry. Folding the removal into the close is the only order that keeps the book until it is on dev. A separate cleanup step after the close would need its own status row with nowhere left to write it, so the key is retired rather than renumbered.

summary: Ship Step 13 runs bkit branches sync-dev: fetch, fast-forward local dev without a checkout (merge --ff-only plus frozen install only when the main checkout is on dev and dev moved); local dev commits missing from origin/dev are logged with the publish command and never pushed. The step key stays ship-switch-to-dev.
description: Local dev commits ahead of origin/dev are someone's unreviewed work; ship is not the place to publish them, and the old rebase-and-push of all-skip-CI commits could still publish them unreviewed. Keeping the frozen step key avoids resetting attempt counters and orphaning the status-hole corpus.

summary: A ship FAILED record whose dev push is refused or exhausted is not landed: workflows handover --flush exits 10 / 11 and the record stays in the book root, where the next ship of {FID} carries it into its own dev commit. No PR fallback and no dev lock.
description: A failure record is low value next to the failure comment already on the issue, and a PR per failure would add review noise. Accepted cost: in an ephemeral cloud container the book dies with the container, so a refused FAILED record there is lost.

summary: bkit roadmap mirror (build / debug close) lands its row through pushToDev in every runtime and skips only when the run's own checkout is on dev; any refusal skips with a log line and exit 0, never a PR.
description: The feat-side row already reaches dev with ship's merge, so the mirror only makes the board current sooner; it must never fail or block a close.

summary: Design / plan / build / debug Failure Paths always keep the run's record through one `workflows handover --push --worktree`: committed and pushed on the feature branch (never onto an open PR); from a dev / main / detached checkout only the logs and ledgers land on dev through pushToDev, nothing committed in the checkout. Ship keeps its --flush to dev.
description: Before, design / plan never committed a failure record and build / debug committed one only with a handover, so a record lived only in a local worktree and died with a cloud container. Debug adopting dev ran `git add -A` + push on dev, publishing the half-done fix and any local-only dev commits. The feature branch is the record's home because code and bookkeeping reach dev together only through ship's merge; dev / main has no feature branch, so only bookkeeping lands there.

summary: No close reads the tracker, because nothing on the board comes from the tracker
description: No phase close reads the tracker, runs a drift check, or evaluates a cadence. Every phase close appends its `kind:"feature"` row to `.bkit/issues.jsonl` and re-renders the roadmap-status block from the ledger through `appendFeature` (`.bkit/core/engine/commands/workflow/roadmap.ts`): design / plan inside `bkit branches land`; build / debug via `bkit roadmap mirror` (the feat-side row, then a dev-side copy landed through a throwaway `origin/dev` checkout, skipped with a log line when the push is refused or fails); ship Step 6 via `bkit roadmap feature --strict`. Rendering is fail-open. Only ship gates on it: `--strict` exits 1 when the `SHIPPED` row could not be appended, and the step routes that to the Failure Path.
rationale: The question of whether a close should enrich from the tracker disappears once the board holds no tracker-derived rows to enrich.

references: .bkit/workflows.md (One landing routine for every dev write; PR-mode design/plan closes MUST push before `bkit prs open`; `[skip ci]` scope; Cross-step invariants: Close squash)
summary: #341 OQ-A confirmed, OQ-D withdrawn: design/plan close lands through `bkit branches land` as a direct dev push of a squash built off origin/dev in every runtime, else (push refused) via a {BRANCH}->dev PR merged with gh (D5(a), not push_files); the landed subject keeps `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no CI

Every runtime first tries the direct close (`landDirect` / `buildClose`): `git merge --squash -X ours {BRANCH}` in a throwaway `.worktrees/_land-{FID}` off a fresh origin/dev, roadmap row, one path-scoped `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` commit (`--squash-of={BRANCH}`), `git push origin HEAD:dev`, rebuilt and retried when dev moved (decision `design-plan-close-throwaway-origin-dev-worktree`). Any other push refusal (branch protection or a ruleset on dev) takes `landPr`: commit the roadmap update on {BRANCH}, push it, open or reuse the {BRANCH}->dev PR (`existing: "reuse"`), and squash-merge it with subject `docs({FID}): <phase> DONE bkit [skip ci]` and an empty body via gh, retrying a refused merge after `update-branch`; exit 80 at stage `open` / `merge` hands either step to MCP `create_pull_request` / `merge_pull_request`, then re-runs with `--pr` / `--merged-sha`; the landed SHA is the PR merge commit. Both paths then scan the landed commit BODY (subject excluded) and cross-check the transport; the `close-transport` row (`closeTransportRow`) is written only on a runtime that does not push dev, whose checkout holds the branch; a runtime that pushes dev never writes the main checkout, logs the skip, and `bkit branches land`'s JSON output carries the same shape, SHA and scan result. The merge does not wait for CI: the landed subject carries `bkit [skip ci]`, so a docs-only close dispatches no run. The OQ-D CI-cost reversal accepted at build (drop `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject) is withdrawn.
rationale: Spike B (closed, folded into the design) found push_files (D5) cannot express `merge --squash -X ours`, inlines full file content per call (non-repairable payload bloat), and inverts conflict semantics (branch-wins vs dev-wins) -- three defects that demote it from primary. D5(a) is uniform with ship's server-side merge and avoids the push_files payload/conflict/credential-coupling defects. OQ-D was reversed: a deliberate `bkit [skip ci]` on a docs-only SUBJECT is the CI-minutes convention. The real defect is a token inherited into a squash BODY; every close passes an explicit --body "" and `bkit prs scan-body` scans the landed BODY only. `.bkit/core/engine/audits/workflows/skip-ci-subject-audit.test.ts` asserts both halves.
alternatives: D5 (push_files) as shape-A primary -- REJECTED per Spike B (non-repairable payload bloat, conflict-semantics inversion, credential coupling shared with gh's own flaky mode-3 auth). Dropping `[skip ci]` from every phase-close and intermediate status subject (the original OQ-D) -- REJECTED on reversal: one full dev CI run per docs-only close; the inherited-token risk is met by an explicit empty squash body plus a landed-body scan.

summary: #384 ship-bookkeeping lands AFTER #341 (d64ef5be merged); 384 re-derives against the post-#341 bkit-ship.md — outcome: 341-first-landed
description: Pre-flight gate for #384 (ship bookkeeping mutates validated PR head). #341 (CLOSED, merged d64ef5be) landed the post-#341 ship markers first: the ship runtime-resolved row writer is present once at bkit-ship.md:320 at d64ef5be, now `bkit runtime row --workflow=ship` at .bkit/core/workflows/bkit-ship.md, RUNTIME_DEVPUSHES appears 10x. #384 takes the post-#341 bkit-ship.md as its diff base: `git log --oneline d64ef5be..HEAD -- .bkit/core/workflows/bkit-ship.md` is empty (no intervening rewrite). No concurrent PR/branch rewrites bkit-ship.md — feat/58-workflow-counters and worktree-374-test-lane-coverage carry 0 bkit-ship.md-touching commits past origin/dev. Ship never checks out dev: Step 13 runs `bkit branches sync-dev`, which fast-forwards local dev without a checkout (decision `ship-sync-dev-fast-forward-only-never-push-local-dev`). Comment corrections folded into issue context by design phase: (a) non-firing pull_request on a CONFLICTING PR is general GitHub behaviour, not a bkit token quirk; (b) cancel-in-progress is a second independent justification for the frozen head; (c) Path B2 is the common case, not the escape hatch.
rationale: Two workflows rewriting bkit-ship.md on the same clone would collide. Recording 341-first-landed makes the serialisation explicit and machine-checkable: any later task asserting it can grep docs/decisions.jsonl for outcome 341-first-landed on key 384-341-serialisation.
alternatives: Land 384 against pre-#341 bkit-ship.md — REJECTED: would re-derive RUNTIME_DEVPUSHES/worktree conventions that #341 already settled. Block 384 behind an open #341 PR — REJECTED: #341 is CLOSED (d64ef5be merged).

summary: Ship keeps its 14 step names (`ship-worktree-cleanup` retired by decision `ship-close-removes-worktree-after-landing`); Steps 3 and 9 write no row and check their values with `steps gate --placeholder`
rationale: The names are frozen by `ship-invariants.test.ts` and `checks/status-holes.ts`; new rows would break the status-hole check for every past ship.

summary: Flags only tests passed are removed; tests set `package.json` `bkit.*` values instead
rationale: Follows 489-no-code-without-a-production-caller. Removed: `runs wait|gate --capstone/--ci-workflow/--required-lanes`, `--tracker` on `prs open` and `issues labels`, `runtime row --at`, `branches switch --lock-wait`, `--context-file`.

summary: Ship's close (docs({FID}): ship DONE) and Failure Path record (chore({FID}): ship FAILED) are built by pushToDev in a throwaway .worktrees/_land-{FID} off origin/dev, carrying the run's book (md logs dev lacks or the run rewrote copied, ledgers unioned; from a dev / main checkout only the run's own record), and pushed as dev with rebuild-and-retry when dev moved. Ship books in {WORKTREE_PATH} in every runtime; its workflow lock stays in the main checkout. The repo-global dev lock, bkit branches switch and every --dev-pushes flag are removed.
description: A laptop ship switched the main checkout to dev and committed there under a dev lock, so it could sweep another session's uncommitted work into its commit and serialised every parallel close. The design / plan close already proved the throwaway-checkout routine; ship now uses the same one, which removes the shared checkout from every dev write and leaves the push as the only race. Logs the run rewrote are copied too, so a second handover updates dev instead of leaving the first copy. The book moves to the feature worktree because the main checkout is no longer a tree ship may write to; the lock stays in the main checkout because it is gitignored and must be one file whichever tree the run books in.

summary: pushToDev runs every git command of a landing with core.hooksPath pointed at the null device (one more GIT_CONFIG_* entry), and logs that hooks were skipped. It is the one named exception to 'workflows never bypass hooks' in .bkit/templates.md.
description: A landing commits only docs, logs and ledger rows under [skip ci], built on a fresh origin/dev the run did not edit. The consumer's pre-commit / pre-push hooks gate code (format, static, unit, bkit check); run in the throwaway they either re-check the whole of dev, which the landing cannot fix, or fail on a checkout with no installed dependencies, so a hook failure would strand a close that has nothing for the hook to check. Skipping them is logged so it is never silent.
alternatives: Run the hooks: a red dev or a missing node_modules in the throwaway blocks every close. --no-verify per command: misses hooks git runs outside commit / push (post-checkout on worktree add).

summary: A Failure Path run from a dev / main / detached checkout lands only the run's own record: its log folder (md logs plus that folder's uncommitted .jsonl lines) and shared-ledger lines that are uncommitted and carry workflow == this workflow and ts >= the run's workflow-started at. No start row → no shared-ledger row is carried, logged. The hand-back removes exactly the carried lines; staged or since-edited files are kept and named.
description: On a shared checkout the uncommitted ledger lines can belong to another session or to a half-finished fix; carrying every line would publish them as this run's FAILED record, and handing the whole file back would delete them locally. The same workflow-and-time rule already scopes ledgerCounts, so the record and the close telemetry agree on what the run wrote.
alternatives: Carry every uncommitted ledger line (publishes other sessions' rows). Carry only the log folder (loses the run's own decisions and friction rows).

summary: Ship Step 1 runs bkit worktrees setup and bkit workflows start (with status path, ship-start-workflow and runtime row) straight after the workflow lock, before tracker writes and the repo preflight. Step names are unchanged (467-ship-step-names-frozen); lock age is still never checked.
description: Ship books every row in the feature worktree, so a failure between the lock and the worktree had no book: the Failure Path could record nothing and the flush had nothing to land. Opening the run first means every later failure keeps its record. The ship-input file stays in Step 2 because it needs ISSUE_TEXT.

summary: bkit workflows close --flush releases the ship lock only once the close landed on dev or its ship-close/{FID} PR opened. Any other outcome (dev moved before every push, a push with no server answer, fetch / checkout / commit failure, PR not opened) exits non-zero with the lock kept, for the Failure Path.
description: The Failure Path's workflows fail --token releases the lock; a close that had already released it left the Failure Path running unlocked while another ship of the same FID could start.

summary: ghUnavailable counts a failed gh call whose stderr carries HTTP 403 as unavailable, like gh missing or not logged in, so the caller hands the call to the GitHub MCP.
description: The Claude cloud proxy answers gh pr and gh issue (GraphQL) with a 403 (cloud environments docs, GitHub proxy section; inferred, not tested in a session). Before, a 403 was exit 1 and stopped the close's PR route with an error instead of switching to the MCP, which has its own credentials.

summary: bkit install --tracker=<name> re-renders every installed host and needs no host flag.
description: When --tracker= is given, install dispatches the named modules plus every host detectInstalledModules finds. validateModuleFlagsForVerb accepts install with no module flag when --tracker= is set.
rationale: Each host renders tracker-specific commands, agents and MCP entries, while bkit.issueTracker is one value for the repo. Rendering only the named hosts left the others on the old tracker, so bkit check failed right after an install that exited 0. The documented onboarding command bkit install --tracker=github exited 1.
alternatives: (1) Reject a tracker switch unless every installed host is named: REJECTED, it makes the user list hosts bkit already knows. (2) Change the docs to name a host: REJECTED, the stale-host defect stays.

summary: {{DEFAULT_BRANCH}} is the production branch: origin/HEAD, but main when origin/HEAD is dev or unset.
description: resolveDefaultBranch reads git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD through a non-throwing spawnSync and keeps the whole branch name after refs/remotes/origin/. An empty result or dev gives main.
rationale: Every use of the token in managed docs and CI templates means the production branch, beside dev. A repo whose GitHub default is dev (PRs target dev) rendered dev/dev text, and since origin/HEAD is set by some git versions on fetch and not on others, two machines rendered different bytes and the drift gate flipped by machine.
alternatives: (1) A package.json bkit key naming the production branch: DEFERRED, it needs an upgrade migration for repos whose origin/HEAD names another branch. (2) Always main: REJECTED, it breaks repos whose production branch is master.

summary: A release re-runs no test or lint step: the Release workflow keeps only the on-main check, dist freshness and the CHANGELOG block, sets HUSKY=0, and bkit's own pre-push skips the gates for a tag-only push on commits origin already holds.
description: release.yml dropped typecheck, test, format:check, lint:prose and lint:slop and sets HUSKY=0 on the job. The repo .husky/pre-push exits 0 before the delete-only check when every pushed ref is a tag (or tag delete) whose commit a refs/remotes/<remote> branch contains; the shipped template is unchanged.
rationale: The release commit is already gated: its PR passed bkit-tests-check and the merge push to main runs the full CI suite, and release.yml refuses a tag not on origin/main. Measured on v5.3.0: the Test step took 101s and the sliding v{N} tag push took 176s because pnpm install ran husky and the pushed tag fired the full pre-push gate on the runner; the local tag push ran the full gate a third time, and a v5.4.0 tag push was once refused by it on a commit that passed seconds later.
alternatives: (1) Keep the release re-run as defence in depth: REJECTED, the on-main check plus main protection already block an untested commit and the re-run only adds time and flake exposure. (2) Ship the tag-only skip in the template: NOT DONE, consumers may tag commits their CI never gated. (3) git push --no-verify for the sliding tag: REJECTED, HUSKY=0 also stops the hooks being installed at all.

summary: bkit-utility-update-tracker is the one agent allowed to write tracker issue fields: title, labels, board status, priority, size, milestone, parent and blocked-by. It never creates, closes, reopens or comments, never touches bkit:* labels, never sets a done state and never removes a link.
description: Two-Layer Separation keeps tracker calls in workflows; the roadmap utility reads only. The tracker utility is a second, human-invoked exception with field-write grants. Priority and size come from the newest issues audit Proposal, then the template's Ranking Rules and Size Scale; own judgement fills empty fields only and proposes the rest. GitHub blocked-by is written to the body block build reads.
rationale: The issues audit and roadmap only propose; nothing applied their proposals, so the board drifted from the rules. A utility run by a human is the approval, and the hard limits keep its writes to fields a human can undo.
alternatives: Utility writes a change plan and the caller applies it: every run needs a second manual pass the utility could do itself.
Workflow command instead of an agent: tracker hygiene is not a phase and needs no lock, worktree or status row.

summary: /bkit-design Step 3 Grill ends with a draft scenario round: the orchestrator drafts the acceptance scenario (Narrative, Success Criteria, Key Edge Cases, Process Sketch) from the whole context, asks the human to confirm or refine the inferred parts, and records it under a `DRAFT only` label in design-grill-{RUN}.md. bkit-design-generate starts its Acceptance Scenario from the draft and records each change as a Decisions row.
description: The draft round is always the last round and counts toward the 10-round cap, so decision rounds stop at 9. Headless runs and a human stop record the draft labelled as not reviewed by a human. grill=false writes no draft. The plan template is unchanged: it still copies the design's Acceptance Scenario verbatim and the human confirms it at the plan's Acceptance Scenario confirmed box.
rationale: Owner 2026-10-21: the interview ended on a vague 'confirm shared understanding'; a concrete scenario built from the issue, the prompt and the answers gives the human something specific to confirm or correct before any design work. The DRAFT label tells the design agents they may amend it. Changes made by the design get a Decisions row only, no confirmation item, because the human reviews the scenario again at the plan checkbox.
alternatives: Plan may also amend the scenario with each change listed (rejected by owner: plan keeps copying the design verbatim).
Draft round outside the 10-round cap (rejected by owner: it counts).
Design changes to the draft also raise a Risks & Open Questions item for confirmation (rejected by owner: a second sign-off for the same scenario).

summary: Linear workflow writes send labels and state as separate save_issue calls, labels first; each label a transition adds is created first with save_issue_label (workspace label, `already exists` = done); phase start sets the state type `started`; hand-off keeps the state name `In Review` and a team without it logs Unapplied.
description: Verified live on a default Linear team (#646): save_issue rejects the whole call when any state or label name is unknown, valid fields included, and never creates the name. One combined call let a missing In Review state drop bkit:failed on every Failure Path. Separate calls keep labels landing when the state is missing. `started` is a state type every team has whatever its names; In Review has no type of its own, so it stays a name and its absence is tolerated because bkit:merged / bkit:failed carry the hand-off. Workspace labels need no team UUID (save_issue_label takes teamId as a UUID only, while bkit.linearTeam is a key) and apply to every team. Not verified live: workspace label creation and its permission requirements, and save_issue with a retired label.

summary: Template pre-commit only formats; template pre-push runs the deepest push gate package.json declares (`bkit:gate:static-unit-integration`, else `bkit:gate:static-unit`), skips the suite on revert branches, and blocks a [skip ci] HEAD on a branch with an open PR; bkit-repo pre-commit skips the dist check for test-only commits
description: `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-push` runs `bkit:gate:static-unit-integration` when package.json declares it, else `bkit:gate:static-unit` (BKIT_PUSH_GATES in `.bkit/core/engine/install/manifest.ts`), plus the drift gate; E2E, @live and anything reaching a deployed service stay in CI. The integration tier may start local services (a database in Docker). `.bkit/templates/.husky/pre-commit` runs `bkit:gate:format` only, and the `gate-commit-repeats-push` advisory names any script it shares with the push gate. On a revert branch the test tiers are skipped while lint, typecheck, prose and slop:delta still run. A HEAD commit carrying a [skip ci]-class token is blocked when the branch has an open PR (dev/main exempt, gh absent → allow). bkit's own `.husky/pre-commit` runs `bkit:check:dist` only when a non-test `.bkit/core/engine/**/*.ts` is staged; its pre-push bats run self-skips when bats is absent. bkit's own `bkit:gate:static-unit` runs `test:coverage:unit` in place of `pnpm test`, and it declares `bkit:gate:static-unit-integration` (`test:integration`).
rationale: Integration runs on push, not on commit (owner, 2026-10-21): a commit stays seconds, and a push is where a slower check still costs nothing but local time, ahead of a CI round-trip. The gate is opt-in by declaring it, the same "declared = run it" rule `/bkit-build` uses, so a repo whose integration tier needs something only CI has keeps it CI-only by not declaring the gate. Each check runs once: a commit gate that repeats a push check, a unit gate that calls both `pnpm test` and a coverage run, or a unit config that also matches integration files runs the same work twice on every push (found in bkit, app-gether-life and visitfrasercoast-com, 2026-10-21). The hook mirrors CI's deterministic gates so a green push cannot red-CI on them. Gate content lives in package.json so a human push and an agent run enforce the identical set. A revert leaves the tree intentionally inconsistent (deleted files referenced by surviving tests), so the suite is skipped so recovery lands; prose is unaffected by deleted code and slop:delta reports removals as resolved, never added. The workflow CI-Dispatch gate only covers the push it makes at close; the HEAD guard backstops manual pushes, and is conditioned on an open PR so sanctioned [skip ci] pushes with no PR still pass. `bkit:check:dist` rebuilds from the working tree, so a test-only commit made while a source edit is uncommitted would fail on a diff it did not cause. bats is not a devDependency, and without the self-skip a contributor without bats could not push.
